newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Socialists heading for wages showdown. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Socialists heading for wages showdown. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government was heading for a showdown with public sector unions in wage talks beginning on Wednesday (Corrects), with single currency economic goals leaving ministers little room for manoeuvre.

Unions, representing over 500,000 public admininstration workers, are demanding salary increases for 1997 of between 4.5 and seven percent, some two to three times the inflation rate the government is predicting for next year.

Prime Minister Antonio Guterres has warned that Portugal can afford increases in the public sector, which sets the trend for private sector rises, only slightly above the targeted 2.25-2.50 inflation rate.

Any more than that, the government says, would jeopardise Portugal's chances of qualifying for the European Union's planned single currency for which the country must meet tight economic entry tests next year.
The government will spell out its offer at the start of talks on Wednesday afternoon.
According to newspaper reports the initial proposal will be for salary rises of 2.5-3.0 percent but officials could not immediately be contacted to comment.

Union leaders, who say the purchasing power of public sector workers has fallen in recent years, warn of trouble if the government does not agree to rises at least as high as last year's 4.25 percent.
"There will be conflict," union leader Carlos Mamede, head of the 300,000 strong, Communist-led Frente Commun, told Reuters recently when asked to comment on how the unions would respond.
But independent economists are equally adamant that the government cannot afford to stray far from the inflation rate.
While some economists said that the government could go as high as 3.5 percent, a real rise after inflation of one percent, the same as in 1996, others felt that this would be too much.
"Anything above three percent and it would be difficult for the government to achieve its deficit and budget targets," said economist Carla Rebelo of Lisbon's Finantia.
Entry to the EU's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) -- the single currency -- sets a ceiling on members' budget deficits of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) next year.
Inflation can be no more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of the three best-performing countries in the 15-nation bloc.
Portugal has targeted a deficit of 2.9 percent for next year, down from an expected four percent in 1996.
But despite tough talk from the unions, analysts said that the government was going into the negotiations in a fairly strong position.

Portugal has experienced little labour strife since the early 1980s and it is doubtful that the unions really feel strong enough to take on a government that has said it will do everything it has to qualify for EMU, analysts said.
Any wage rise would be better than the prospects facing unions in neighbouring Spain where the government, also battling to meet EMU goals, has decreed a salary freeze, they added.
The government's hand could be strengthened by a recent survey in Lisbon newspaper O Publico showing that the Portuguese are ready for sacrifices to reach the single currency.
